1: Welcome to Module 1 of the Ticket-to-Machine learning path: the loop and the typed task.

This path builds the identity half of the Federal Modernization Workbook's Book 13's Ticket-to-Machine loop on two named products: ServiceNow as the front door and the record, and SailPoint Identity Security Cloud for identity governance.
They're an example, not an endorsement.
This module starts at the guide's Gate 4, because every other gate writes or reads the record that gate defines: the identity finding.
You'll map the kit's files to the loop's five steps, learn the finding's data contract, and check payloads on a laptop the way ServiceNow will, before anything reaches an instance.
2: An access ticket closes when a technician types done.
Nobody can say who owned the drift, when it fell due, or what the account should look like afterward.
Book 13 says an assessor asks four questions about every finding: who owns it, by when, under whose approval, and with what evidence of closure.
A ticket closed on done answers none of them; it records a claim.
Book 13's answer is a typed task: one record with a class, a severity, an owner, a clock, and an intended state that a later re-read can check.
Every step of the loop writes or reads this record, so it's where you start.
3: Here's what you'll be able to do by the end of this module, which takes about fifty minutes with the lab.
You'll explain the loop's five steps and name the file in the kit that performs each one.
You'll describe the fields of the identity finding's data contract and what each one is for.
You'll validate a finding payload on a laptop, and predict whether ServiceNow accepts it, rejects it or de-duplicates it, and when it falls due.
And you'll recognize an intended state that gives the re-read nothing to check.
Before you start, read Book 13's Chapter 10 and skim Appendix B.
For Lab 1 you need Python, Node.js and a Bash-compatible shell.
You don't need a ServiceNow instance or a SailPoint tenant until Lab 2.
4: One, test: a rule evaluates actual state against the authoritative record.
Two, detect drift: a difference becomes a typed finding with a severity.
Three, raise a typed task against the reconciled configuration item, with an owner and a clock.
Four, actuate on the native surface, under a service identity, through the platform's own interface.
And five, close with evidence: re-read the post-change state and write one record of the whole chain.
The coordination layer in front of the native tools never writes the configuration itself.
Its job is to make every drift an owned, clocked, approved and evidenced piece of work.
In the program's model, the ticket authorizes a machine, and the person's role ends at approval.
5: Now map the kit onto that loop.

Step one, test, is the drift client, which joins the H R extract, Microsoft Graph and SailPoint on employee I D. Step two, detect drift, is SailPoint's event triggers, for a native change or an attribute change, plus the drift client.
Step three, raise a typed task, is the SailPoint workflows' HTTP Request step and the Scripted REST resource in ServiceNow, which writes the identity finding table.
Step five, close with evidence, is a business rule that turns any close into Awaiting verification, and the re-read client, which closes only on a re-read.
Actuation has no code in Pass 1: nothing in the kit writes to Entra I D, Active Directory or SailPoint.
You'll meet that step again in Module 6.
6: The example guide shows which product does each step.

For raising a typed task, which is Gate 4, it's a SailPoint workflow posting to a ServiceNow endpoint, which is a build; the Service Catalog app for people's requests; and Service Desk tickets for disconnected applications.
Used as shipped, the two products fall short of the loop in four places.
One: SailPoint's Service Desk integration treats its task as complete from the ServiceNow status, and a ticket status isn't a re-read.
Two: the catalog app moves access approval into ServiceNow.
Three: SailPoint's Service Desk integration raises only service requests and incidents, not change requests.
And four: there are two doors into the directory.
Each gate that closes a gap says so; the slide shows which.
7: Here's the record those steps share: the identity finding, and its data contract.
Kind is a finding, the default, or a closure signal.
Source is SailPoint or the drift reconciliation.
The drift class is one of Book 03's seven classes, and it's required.
Severity is P one to P four; leave it out and it defaults by class, Book 03's High to P two and Medium to P three, which is design guidance.
System says where the re-read happens: a SailPoint account, a SailPoint identity or an Entra user.
One subject identifier is required, and de-duplication uses the first one present.
And the intended state says what a re-read must find; when a SailPoint event arrives without one, the script derives it.
The implementation example maps each field to Book 13's evidence record.
8: The contract is enforced in one place: the Scripted REST resource, which runs inside ServiceNow.
It validates the payload and answers four hundred with the reason when something's wrong.
It maps severity to a priority, one to four, and a due date on the program's tempo.
It de-duplicates against an active finding: when one already has the same source, subject, class and attribute, it answers two hundred with the existing record instead of creating a second.
And when a SailPoint event arrives with no intended state, it derives one.
A new finding gets two oh one, with its number and priority.
Until then, nothing outside ServiceNow applied the same rules, so a client learned that a payload was wrong only from a four hundred on a live instance.
9: Where do the due dates come from?
A P one, critical, isn't fixed by a machine: the run halts and alerts, and a named role decides.
P two, high, has a one-hour window.
And P four, low, seventy-two hours.
The script turns those windows into each record's due date.
These are the program's internal windows, program design, not a federal requirement.
They bound the response, not the occurrence.
And they don't replace external timelines: where a sis-uh directive sets a shorter clock, the external clock governs.
Book 13 also notes that a program with no findings is more likely blind than clean.
10: Chapter 01 adds finding contract dot py, which applies the script's rules on a laptop.

Its validate function returns the errors ServiceNow would answer four hundred to, warnings for what it would accept but the loop can't use, and the normalized values: severity, priority, system, subject, de-duplication key and window.
Its constants mirror the script's, and a test reads the JavaScript and fails if they drift apart.
An intended state of empty attributes and an empty list of entitlements is a non-empty object, so it looks present.
But a re-read finds no difference against it, and would close the record on nothing.
For missing identity and unauthorized write, which Book 13 routes to a person first, the empty intent is expected until that person sets it.
11: Lab 1 runs in the kit's folder, on a laptop, against fictional fixtures, with no tenant.
In step two you check five sample payloads the way the Scripted REST resource would.
Sample one gave no severity, so the class default gave it P two and a one-hour window: due at one o'clock for a run at noon.
Sample two has a typo in its drift class, and sample four has a severity of P five.
Both would get a four hundred, so the command exits one.
Sample three is accepted, but warned: its intended state names nothing a re-read can check, which is expected for an unauthorized write.
And sample five, a closure signal, moves matching findings to Awaiting verification.

14: Gate 4 turns findings and requests into documented, owned, clocked records.
The guide maps it to four controls in nist special publication eight hundred fifty-three.
C M three, configuration change control: every proposed change is a documented, owned record.
R A seven, risk response: findings are answered inside declared windows.
C A seven, continuous monitoring: monitoring results become tracked work.
And A C five, separation of duties: a request passes a separation-of-duties check and an approver who isn't the requester.
The evidence an I S S O keeps from this module: the ServiceNow finding records and the contract tests in the repository, and each record's due date, which Module 7 measures.
Before shipping, work through the chapter's checklist.
15: Check yourself with two questions from the module's knowledge check.
First: a payload has a drift class of stale access and no severity.
What does the Scripted REST resource do?
It accepts it with the class default, P two, and a one-hour window.
The script defaults severity by class, and sample one in the lab showed exactly that.
Second: what does a closure signal payload do to matching findings?
It moves them to Awaiting verification, and it never closes them.
Only a re-read closes a finding.
The module page has two more questions, each linked to the section that answers it.
